clue.text: Eagerly buy something worthless on back of tin

indicators.note: Riding on the back of something means coming along behind it, so the worthless item's letters trail the metal rather than lead it.

parts.note: the chemical symbol for tin, element 50 on the periodic table
to be sold a pup is to be fobbed off with a worthless thing, and the idiom keeps its article

explanation.surface: A shopper keenly buying a bit of junk stuck to the back of a can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin' is the metal rather than the container, and metals reach cryptics as their periodic-table symbols. The pup is the swindler's classic worthless goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Eagerly buy -> SNAP UP: to snap something up is to buy it fast, before anyone else can, with the eagerness built into the phrase.

clue.text: Turning point for the sun going up and down

indicators.note: in a down entry the word reads the same going up as going down, so it is a palindrome

parts.note: midday is when the sun stops climbing and starts to sink

explanation.surface: The sun's daily arc reaches its peak, rising and setting.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is also the wordplay: the word for midday reads the same upward and downward in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: At midday the sun reaches its highest point and begins to descend, the turning point of its daily path.

clue.text: Not amused picking up work after ineffective coffee

indicators.note: Anything picked up in a down entry travels back towards the top, so the letters assembled below arrive in the opposite order.
Coming after something puts it behind, so the work sits at the tail of the coffee before the pair is lifted.

parts.note: coffee with the caffeine taken out does not do coffee's job
an op is a work, the same shortening as a composer's opus

explanation.surface: A humourless employee collecting a job after a cup of coffee that did nothing for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picking up' reads as collecting the work and is the instruction that turns the whole assembly over, both pieces at once rather than either on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Not amused -> PO-FACED: po-faced means humourless and disapproving, wearing the solemn expression of someone refusing to see the joke.

clue.text: Walk before comprehending warning notice

indicators.note: To comprehend something is to take it in and hold it there, so what follows lands inside the word doing the comprehending.

parts.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before, and the three letters open up after the second
an omen is a sign that warns of what is coming
a notice in a paper is an ad, the classified sort

explanation.surface: Strolling along before you take in a sign telling you to keep off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warning notice' looks like one object on a post and is two separate words to translate. The definition is a noun as well as a verb: the seafront kind you walk along.
explanation.definitionFit: Walk -> PROMENADE: a promenade is both the paved walk along a seafront and the leisurely stroll you take on it.

clue.text: New tipi soon standing

indicators.note: New means made afresh, and letters remade from scratch have no obligation to come back in the order they were handed over.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A freshly pitched tipi that will soon be up and standing on the campsite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' reads as the tent staying upright and means status instead - the rank someone holds in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: standing -> POSITION: both are nouns for the rank or status someone holds, as in a position of authority or standing in the community.

clue.text: Painter really in friend's shade

indicators.note: Being in a friend rather than beside one puts the pieces just named between that friend's letters.

parts.note: a pal is a friend, and the three letters part after the second
an RA is a Royal Academician, a painter elected to London's Royal Academy
so tired is really tired, the word working as an intensifier

explanation.surface: A painter genuinely overshadowed by a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shade' is where the trap sits: it reads as the shadow one artist casts over another, and it means the thing that makes shade.
explanation.definitionFit: shade -> PARASOL: a parasol is carried to make shade, so the setter defines it by what it produces rather than what it is made of.

clue.text: Insane jockeys having no end of fun here?

indicators.note: jockeys as a verb means manoeuvres or jostles, so the letters are shifted about
having no means one letter is taken out of the pool before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the last letter of fun

explanation.surface: Crazy riders, all fun drained away, might race here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of fun' is N; 'having no' takes it out of INSANE, and 'jockeys' rearranges what is left. Siena's Palio is a famously wild bareback horse race round its main square, hence the jockeys.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian city stages the Palio, a reckless horse race, so it is the place where insane jockeys compete.

clue.text: Oven with duck in to roast, initially

indicators.note: in places the conjunction and the duck inside the word to

parts.note: taken as written
and joins things together, as with does
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, shaped like O

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of roast

parts.note: the first letter of roast

explanation.surface: A cook puts a duck in the oven to roast it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' (AND) and 'duck' (O) go 'in' TO, giving TANDOO; 'roast, initially' adds R. A duck is a cricket score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandoor is a clay oven used in Indian and Pakistani cooking.

clue.text: Upset voter rattled ballot box — Lib Dem leader?

indicators.note: rattled means shaken up, so the letters of voter are jumbled

parts.note: an urn is a ballot box, especially in French elections
Ed Davey leads the UK Liberal Democrats

explanation.surface: An angry voter shook the ballot box, perhaps the Lib Dem leader himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' at the front looks like a description of the voter, but it is the definition. Ed Davey leads the Liberal Democrats, a British political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Overturned means knocked over, the physical sense of upset, as in an upset cart.

clue.text: Holes beginning to grow naturally around lake

definitions.note: A golf course is one place, and the setter names it by the eighteen holes it is made of, so a plural definition stands for a singular answer.

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its first letter, and 'beginning to grow' asks for no more of that word than its start.

parts.note: the first letter of grow, and nothing more of it

indicators.note: What goes around something encloses it, so the letters named before this close over the lake instead of sitting beside it.

parts.note: naturally means of course, and the phrase opens up after its first letter
L is the map-maker's short form for a lake

explanation.surface: Holes that have started to appear of their own accord in the ground round a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naturally' looks like an adverb describing how the holes are spreading, and it is a two-word phrase waiting to be spelled out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: Holes -> GOLF COURSE: a course is its eighteen holes taken together, so the setter names the place by the only feature that counts on it.

clue.text: Want massage from lecturer?

indicators.note: A lecturer delivers everything out loud, so a word arriving from one reaches you as a sound and may be spelled quite differently.

parts.note: to massage dough or a stiff shoulder is to knead it, and the opening K goes silent as soon as you say the word

explanation.surface: Fancying a massage, and the unlikely thought of getting one from your lecturer.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K is the whole trick. 'Want' works as noun or verb, and so does the answer, so the definition fits whichever way you read the clue's first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Want -> NEED: both name what you lack and must have, though need carries more urgency than a mere wish does.

clue.text: Elasticated foot warmers from chemist on King's Road?

indicators.note: A shop described as on a road stands along it, so in an across entry the chemist's letters take up position after the road's.

parts.note: the King's Road is the long shopping street that runs through Chelsea in west London
Boots is the chemist on nearly every British high street

explanation.surface: Stretchy footwear bought at the chemist's shop on the King's Road.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are proper names dressed as plain description, a shop and a street, and the footwear took its name from that same corner of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Elasticated foot warmers -> CHELSEA BOOTS: ankle boots with an elastic gusset at each side, which is what lets you pull them on without laces.

clue.text: Cunning to take group on board chopper

indicators.note: Taking something in is holding it inside you, so what the cunning takes ends up between its letters.

parts.note: guile is cunning, and the five letters part after the fourth
a lot is a group of people or things taken together
a passenger on board a boat is in it

explanation.surface: Cleverly getting a whole party on board a helicopter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chopper' is the helicopter the group are boarding on the surface and a machine that chops in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: chopper -> GUILLOTINE: a guillotine chops, whether it is taking off heads or trimming a ream of paper, so the blunt word covers it.

clue.text: Cold plain fish sandwiches outside for docker

indicators.note: To sandwich something is to put it between two slices, so the fish closes over the letters named next.

parts.note: tuna is the fish, and the four letters open up before the last

indicators.note: The outside of a word is its first and last letters, and that pair is all this hands over.

parts.note: the first and last letters of docker, the pair on the outside

explanation.surface: Plain fish sandwiches served cold and outdoors to a man working the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' is the verb, not the lunch, and 'Cold plain' is two words of a single definition rather than a description of the food.
explanation.definitionFit: Cold plain -> TUNDRA: the treeless Arctic flat where the subsoil never thaws, which is a cold plain and little else.

clue.text: Writer's arty novel rarely containing sex?

indicators.note: containing means the rearranged letters hold the next piece inside them
novel means new, so the letters of rarely are made into a new arrangement

parts.note: it is an old euphemism for sex or sex appeal

explanation.surface: A writer's high-brow novel rarely includes sex scenes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like part of the book picture but is the anagram signal. IT for sex appeal comes from the 1920s 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary describes things to do with writers and books, and often suggests something cultured or artistic.

clue.text: Something nasty in your mug as well — husband cutting facial hair?

parts.note: as well means too, and it takes the front

indicators.note: Cutting into something opens a gap in it, and the letter named just before this drops into the gap.

parts.note: a tache is a moustache, clipped the way British speech clips it, and the five letters open up after the first
H is the standard short form of husband, as on a form

explanation.surface: Something unpleasant floating in your cup, and a husband trimming his moustache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mug' is the cup you are drinking from until you remember it is British slang for a face, and the nasty thing is in your teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nasty in your mug -> TOOTHACHE: mug is slang for the face, and a bad tooth is about the nastiest thing a face can be holding.

clue.text: Joey's father's packing large knickers

indicators.note: Packing something means stowing it inside, so the letter named next slots into the word doing the packing.

parts.note: a joey is a young kangaroo and the adult male of the species is a boomer; the possessive s supplies the last letter
L is the clothing size, as printed on the label

explanation.surface: Joey's dad packing a large pair of underwear for the trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joey' looks like a boy's name and is a kangaroo cub; boomer for the adult male is Australian usage rather than crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: knickers -> BLOOMERS: the loose gathered drawers Victorian women wore, and still the joke word for voluminous knickers.

clue.text: Suspicious article covered with ground nuts

indicators.note: covered with means the article is wrapped inside the rearranged letters
nuts means crazy, so the letters of ground are scrambled

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A wary diner eyes an item coated in crushed nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' scrambles GROUND to ONGURD, and the article A is 'covered with' it: ONGU-A-RD. 'ground nuts' reads like a food, but 'nuts' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on guard is to be watchful and wary, alert to possible danger or deceit.

clue.text: Bite dog, perhaps after son bit

indicators.note: Coming after something puts you behind it, so the son's letter takes the top of a down entry and the rest queue up below.

parts.note: S is the standard short form of son, as in a family record
a nip is a small sharp bite
'perhaps' marks definition by example: a dog is one kind of pet

explanation.surface: A dog that has nipped the son, and the thought of biting it back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit' is the definition, sitting at the end where it reads as part of the story - the size of the bite rather than a piece of news.
explanation.definitionFit: bit -> SNIPPET: a snippet is a small piece snipped off something bigger, usually of news or talk, which is exactly a bit of it.

clue.text: Lots love line in poetry

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, and nil is written as a nought

indicators.note: A poem is made of lines, so a line that is in poetry goes inside those letters rather than alongside them.

parts.note: odes are poetry, and the four letters open up after the second
L is the short form of line, as on a railway map

explanation.surface: Plenty of people love a good line of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots love' reads as a crowd of admirers, and each of those words is doing another job: one is the definition, the other a nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Lots -> OODLES: oodles is the informal word for a great quantity, and like lots it takes a plural verb after it.

clue.text: Reject managed to conceal stigma

indicators.note: Anything concealed is hidden inside something bigger, so the stigma disappears between the letters that hide it.

parts.note: if you managed it, you did it, and the three letters part after the second
a scar is the mark an injury leaves, and a stigma is that mark on a reputation

explanation.surface: Someone who has managed to keep a shameful mark hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: The plainest word in the clue is the one carrying letters: 'managed' is a past tense standing in for another past tense rather than describing anybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Reject -> DISCARD: to discard is to throw out what you no longer want, a card from your hand or a plan from a meeting.

clue.text: Show disapproval of wobbly thingies on German porn film

indicators.note: on says the jeer is placed first, with the rest of the letters set after it

parts.note: boo is the jeer of a disapproving crowd

indicators.note: wobbly means unsteady, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone jeers at jiggling objects in a German adult film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wobbly thingies' paints a risqué image, but 'wobbly' only signals a rearrangement, and 'on' sets the jeer first.
explanation.definitionFit: Boogie Nights is the 1997 Paul Thomas Anderson film about the pornography industry.

clue.text: Cream filling for her diet

indicators.note: The filling of a sandwich is the bit in the middle, so what is wanted from the word after it is its middle letter.

parts.note: the middle letter of the three
lite is how the label spells the diet version of a drink or a snack

explanation.surface: Cream filling in a pudding that is meant to be part of her diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cream' is not dairy: the cream of something is its best part. 'Filling' looks like the middle of a cake and is an instruction about the middle of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream -> ELITE: the cream of a group is its choicest few, which is what an elite is - the pick of the crop.

clue.text: That stinks in a similar way to sulphur

parts.note: a la is the borrowed French for in the manner of, familiar from a la carte
S is sulphur's symbol in the periodic table

explanation.surface: A smell being compared to the reek of sulphur.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is today's grumble standing in for an old-fashioned cry of regret, which is why it hides so well at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: That stinks -> ALAS: alas is the cry for something gone wrong, which is what 'that stinks' says in modern slang.

clue.text: Princess up against a woman that acts like one

parts.note: Princess Diana was Di in every headline of the eighties and nineties
two sides up against each other are written with a v between them, short for versus
the word taken as the single letter it is

explanation.surface: A princess squaring up to a woman with airs of her own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' at the end points back at the princess, so the definition is a woman who behaves as though she were royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: woman that acts like one -> DIVA: a diva is a star who carries on with the grandeur of a princess and expects to be treated as one.

clue.text: Free of sin, one's fit to be kissed in audience

parts.note: one's is I am, which shortens to two letters

indicators.note: An audience takes everything in by ear, so the phrase before it is wanted as a sound and comes out spelled another way.

parts.note: a peck is a quick kiss, so anything fit for one is peckable

explanation.surface: Being sinless, and worth a kiss in front of everybody watching.
explanation.walkthrough: The word you hear is a real one: peccable means liable to sin, from Latin peccare, so the negative prefix on the front of it means exactly what the definition says.
explanation.definitionFit: Free of sin -> IMPECCABLE: literally not able to sin, and now used of anything faultless - manners, timing, a performance.

clue.text: Bum numb? Perhaps cane …

parts.note: a numb limb is dead - you feel nothing in it
'perhaps' marks definition by example: caning is one way of beating somebody

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a numbed backside calls for a caning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' is the definition and the joke at once: the American noun for a loafer sitting next to the British one for a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Bum -> DEADBEAT: a deadbeat is an idle sponger who never pays their way, which is what bum means in American usage.

clue.text: … mark remains on bottom

indicators.note: In an across entry what sits on something else is written after it, so the remains follow the bottom.

parts.note: the bottom of a list is its end
what remains of a fire is ash

explanation.surface: The mark left at the bottom where something has burned away.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces break one letter later than the answer does, which is what makes them so hard to see. An en is the printer's width of a letter N, and it names this dash.
explanation.definitionFit: mark -> EN DASH: a punctuation mark one en wide, the dash printers use for ranges such as 1914-18.
